title: Neutrinos: Why These Ghost Particles Matter
excerpt: Astronomers are detecting more and more neutrinos from deep space, opening a new window to the Universe
content:
Max Planck Society

Astronomers are detecting more and more neutrinos from deep space, opening a new window to the Universe

Francis Halzen's Nobel Prize in Physics has put neutrinos in the spotlight. What makes these elusive elementary particles so special? Research at Max Planck Institutes points to an answer: Neutrinos open a new window to the universe.

Billions of neutrinos pass through us all the time and we never even notice. These electrically neutral elementary particles have a vanishingly small mass. Produced by high-energy processes, including those in space, they travel at almost the speed of light. Because neutrinos interact with matter only through the weak nuclear force and gravity, they usually pass straight through it. They pass through stars, planets, and even people. Every second, billions of neutrinos pass through every square centimeter of our bodies, without us ever feeling a thing.

Yet scientists can detect these "ghost particles." And it's important that they can, because the particles carry clues to some of the key processes at work in the cosmos. Catching them, though, takes a huge effort. This year, the Nobel Prize in Physics has gone to Francis Halzen for his life's work: the IceCube neutrino detector in Antarctica. This extraordinary instrument is being used by a large research collaboration to detect high-energy neutrinos arriving from deep space.

Hunting neutrinos in Antarctica

Most neutrinos detected on Earth don't have that much energy. Many form in the atmosphere when protons and other charged particles in cosmic rays strike atomic nuclei in the air, triggering showers of secondary particles. These showers also produce neutrinos. Others stream constantly from the Sun, where nuclear fusion produces lower-energy neutrinos. Cosmic neutrinos, by contrast, can travel millions or even billions of light-years to reach us, carrying information from parts of the universe that remain largely unexplored.

To pick out these cosmic visitors, IceCube relies on highly sensitive optical sensors. Suspended on cables in 86 boreholes at depths of roughly 1,500 to 2,500 meters, the sensors monitor a cubic kilometer of clear Antarctic ice. Every few months, somewhere in this enormous block of ice, a cosmic neutrino strikes a proton or neutron instead of passing through the ice without a trace.

When that happens, the particles interact-sometimes producing a negatively charged muon. Muons resemble electrons, but they are heavier. As a charged muon races through water, it produces a flash of light: a phenomenon known as Cherenkov radiation. The flash is invisible to the naked eye, but IceCube's sensors can detect it. The pattern and brightness of the light trail reveal the original neutrino's kinetic energy and direction of travel. That is what makes neutrinos so useful to astronomers: They have no electric charge and rarely interact with matter along the way, so they stay on course, allowing researchers to trace them back to their source and investigate the processes taking place there. Light, by contrast, can be scattered or dimmed by clouds of gas in space.

Where do the highest-energy neutrinos come from?

This is where the Max Planck Society comes in. Although it is not directly involved in IceCube, the society's Institutes for Nuclear Physics, Radio Astronomy, and Physics make important contributions to understanding neutrinos and their properties. One key interest of the research teams is light arriving on Earth from the same direction as a neutrino at around the same time. Detecting that light requires instruments and telescopes different from those used to detect neutrinos. This approach is known as multimessenger astronomy.

Whenever IceCube reports a cosmic neutrino, astronomers around the world point their telescopes toward the relevant patch of sky. "We have access to several instruments that let us check whether anything unusual is happening at other wavelengths in the same direction," says Eduardo Ros of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Bonn. His team uses the Effelsberg Radio Telescope in Germany's Eifel region, for example, to observe these areas of the sky at low radio frequencies, working closely with a team at the University of Würzburg.

At the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics, director Jim Hinton and his team specialize in high-frequency gamma rays. They use the H.E.S.S. telescopes in Namibia to search for high-energy gamma radiation, while colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Physics use the MAGIC telescope on La Palma. Unlike an ordinary optical telescope, a gamma-ray telescope does not simply collect visible light: It detects secondary particles in the atmosphere that are produced by gamma rays. When a gamma-ray photon strikes a particle in the Earth's atmosphere, it triggers a shower of secondary particles, and as those particles travel through the air, they generate brief flashes of Cherenkov light. The shape of the resulting shower helps astronomers work out where the gamma rays came from. "Ideally, our observations line up, allowing us to identify a source responsible for the signals detected across all these channels," Hinton says.

Supermassive black holes: neutrino factories?

The prime suspects are active galactic nuclei. At the centers of large, distant galaxies, supermassive black holes swallow huge amounts of matter, often launching jets of charged particles into space. A working group at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Bonn is investigating how these jets form and how they produce high-energy neutrinos. These enormous systems are especially intriguing because they are thought to be engines of cosmic evolution: They grow alongside their host galaxies, evolve over timescales approaching the age of the universe, and have profoundly shaped its history as powerful sources of energy.

Neutrinos from these objects could reveal what other observations cannot: "Many originate close to the black hole, in regions where light is completely absorbed," Hinton says. "Gamma rays and radio waves from those regions can't reach us to tell us what is happening." And that's what makes high-energy neutrinos so valuable.

In two prominent cases, researchers have already found fairly strong statistical evidence linking neutrinos to active galactic nuclei: In 2017, a single high-energy neutrino coincided with a gamma-ray outburst from the blazar TXS 0506+056, whose jet points directly toward Earth. Then, in 2022, researchers linked roughly 80 neutrinos to the active galaxy NGC 1068. Rather than hinging on one exceptional detection, the evidence came from the combined pattern of neutrinos arriving from that direction. In recent years, astronomers have identified other individual active galactic nuclei as possible neutrino sources, as well as statistical links between neutrinos and entire catalogs of these galaxies. It seems neutrinos could help us explore the entire universe.

To detect more neutrinos, researchers are building much larger detectors: A second-generation IceCube is planned, with additional strings of sensors expanding the volume of ice it monitors to eight cubic kilometers.

The ANTARES neutrino observatory off the southern coast of France is also being expanded, with similar sensors suspended deep in the Mediterranean scanning the surrounding seawater for flashes of light. The expanded facility, now known as KM3NeT, also has an installation off the coast of Sicily dedicated to cosmic neutrinos. In 2023, it detected the most energetic neutrino recorded to date: a particle with a kinetic energy of 220 petaelectronvolts, or 220 quadrillion electronvolts. That is 16,000 times the energy reached by protons in the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, the world's most powerful particle accelerator. An electronvolt is the energy an electron gains when accelerated through an electric potential difference of one volt.

"Of course we want to know which processes in the cosmos can accelerate particles to such extreme energies," Ros says. "And whether even higher energies are possible." Besides active galactic nuclei, Hinton adds, other sources may emerge: exploding stars, rapidly spinning neutron stars, and so-called microquasars. Microquasars are black holes only a few times the mass of the Sun. Some occur in the Milky Way, where they launch smaller jets. With IceCube, then, a whole new field of research has opened up, giving astronomers another window on the universe. "The Nobel Prize is absolutely deserved," says Hinton, who works closely with Francis Halzen.

Understanding neutrino physics here on Earth

Meanwhile, Max Planck scientists are using experiments on Earth to probe the still-mysterious properties of neutrinos themselves. One unanswered question is their absolute mass. The KATRIN experiment, conducted at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology with contributions from the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics, has so far set an upper limit of 0.45 electronvolts. Such tiny particle masses are impractical to express in grams, but because mass is a form of energy, physicists instead use the energy a particle has when it is at rest.

The TRISTAN experiment is investigating whether a fourth type of neutrino, called a sterile neutrino, exists alongside the familiar electron, muon, and tau neutrinos. Like any particle with mass, a sterile neutrino would be affected by gravity. "That would even make neutrinos candidates for dark matter," says Susanne Mertens, who studies the properties of neutrinos. She is also a director at the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics. Dark matter is one of physics' greatest mysteries: Scientists are certain it exists, and its gravitational influence can be seen in the motion of galaxies within large galaxy clusters. Yet it appears not to interact with light; nor does it emit, deflect or absorb it. Invisible matter might therefore be a more fitting name than dark matter. No one knows what it is made of.

So far, neutrino research has earned five Nobel Prizes: one for the first direct detection of a neutrino; one for the discovery of the muon neutrino; one for the detection of solar neutrinos; one for discovering that neutrinos oscillate, changing from one type to another as they travel, such as from an electron neutrino to a muon neutrino; and, most recently, one for high-energy neutrinos and the IceCube experiment. That so many Nobel Prizes have gone to neutrino research suggests just how much these particles can still teach us about fundamental physics and the universe.
